finding.claim: Stored SSRF (Check 4), MEDIUM. The icon URL submitted via PUT /profile is stored without validation and later fetched by the nightly sync job with a GET. The attacker controls scheme, host and port, so they can target internal or link-local services such as http://169.254.169.254/. The response is read as bytes and not returned to the caller, so this is blind SSRF. The webhook URL on the same path is not vulnerable.
finding.source: `icon` parameter of PUT /profile, Profile.update(String webhook, String icon) at src/Profile.java:11. The caller is assumed to be an authenticated profile owner, though no auth code is in the repo.
finding.sink: HttpClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create(iconUrl)).GET().build(), BodyHandlers.ofByteArray()) at src/Profile.java:23-24, run from the nightly sync() job.

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives the attacker-controlled icon.
this.iconUrl = icon; the value is stored with no validation. The regex check at line 12 covers only webhook.
The nightly job sync(HttpClient c) later reads the stored field.
URI.create(iconUrl) is passed to the request builder and sent with GET. The body is not returned to the user (blind).

finding.guards_checked: No validation of iconUrl at store time (line 16) or fetch time (line 23). There is no scheme or host allowlist, no IP/CIDR block and no egress config in the repo. The HttpClient is injected, so its redirect policy is unknown (JDK default is NEVER). Checked and closed: webhookUrl (lines 12 and 21) is guarded by the anchored full-string regex https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}, which fixes scheme and host, so it is not flagged.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the attacker-supplied icon with no validation (the anchored regex at line 12 covers only webhook), and src/Profile.java:23 fetches it with GET, so a blind SSRF exists; the only attacker requirement is being an authenticated profile owner.
